latent_mechanisms.display_name: Focal Staphylococcus aureus / Group A Streptococcus burden at colonized or infected site
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bacterial proliferation at the toxin-producing focus (vagina/tampon, surgical wound, nasal packing, postpartum uterus, soft tissue, pharynx, varicella lesion). Drives all downstream toxin release; without source control it persists despite antibiotics.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Superantigen elaboration (TSST-1, staphylococcal enterotoxins B/C, streptococcal SpeA/SpeC/SSA)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Toxin secretion by the focal organism. Active protein synthesis is required, which is why ribosomally acting agents (clindamycin, linezolid) are central even when the organism is already β-lactam-susceptible. Suppression of this mechanism is what differentiates toxin-mediated illness control from organism eradication.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: MHC-II / TCR Vβ-restricted polyclonal T cell activation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Superantigens cross-link MHC class II on APCs to specific Vβ regions of the T cell receptor outside the peptide groove, activating up to 5–30% of circulating T cells (vs ~0.01% for conventional antigens). This is the proximate trigger of the cytokine storm.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Massive TNF-α / IL-1 / IL-2 / IL-6 / IFN-γ release
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cytokine cascade driven by Vβ T cell activation and macrophage co-stimulation. Generates fever, vasodilation, capillary leak, and direct tissue toxicity; underlies multi-organ failure pattern.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Distributive shock with profound capillary leak
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cytokine-driven loss of vascular tone plus endothelial leak produces hypotension refractory to modest fluid loading. TSS is one of the most fluid-avid distributive shocks, often requiring 10–20 L crystalloid in the first 24 h.

Toxin-mediated cutaneous vasodilation and superficial inflammation producing the pathognomonic generalized blanching erythema. Followed 1–2 weeks later by characteristic full-thickness palmoplantar desquamation.

Convalescent full-thickness peeling of palms, soles, and digits 7–21 days after acute illness. Retrospectively confirmatory finding; absence does not exclude TSS but presence in the right context is highly specific.

Non-purulent injection of conjunctivae, strawberry tongue, oropharyngeal erythema, and vaginal hyperemia in menstrual TSS. Helps distinguish TSS from bacterial sepsis and overlaps phenotypically with Kawasaki disease/MIS.
Early prominent GI manifestation in staphylococcal TSS; helps distinguish from purely bacteremic septic shock. Can produce significant hypovolemia compounding distributive shock.
Severe diffuse muscle pain with CK rise, contributing to acute kidney injury via pigment nephropathy. CK >2x ULN is a CDC criterion.
Mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic transaminitis with bilirubin elevation, contributed by direct cytokine toxicity, ischemic shock liver, and rhabdomyolysis-driven AST.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Acute kidney injury (prerenal + ATN + pigment nephropathy)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Multifactorial AKI from distributive hypoperfusion, capillary leak, direct toxin/cytokine injury, and myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis. Frequently requires renal replacement therapy in severe cases.

Endothelial activation and tissue factor release, particularly prominent in streptococcal TSS. Manifests as thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/aPTT, hypofibrinogenemia, and elevated D-dimer; can progress to purpura fulminans.
Capillary leak in pulmonary microvasculature plus cytokine-mediated alveolar injury. Common reason for mechanical ventilation in TSS; aggravated by large-volume resuscitation.

Disorientation, agitation, or depressed consciousness from cytokine toxicity and hypoperfusion, in the absence of focal deficits or meningismus. Distinguishes TSS from bacterial meningitis/encephalitis.

Deep soft-tissue infection with fascial necrosis. Pain out of proportion to exam, woody induration, dusky/violaceous skin, bullae, crepitus. Associated with ~50% of streptococcal TSS; mandates emergent surgical debridement.
Streptococcal TSS is bacteremic in ~60% of cases; staphylococcal TSS is bacteremic in only ~5%. Therefore negative blood cultures do not exclude staphylococcal TSS.

Retained tampon, undebrided necrotizing fasciitis, retained nasal packing, undrained postpartum uterine focus, or undrained surgical wound abscess. Without source control, antibiotics alone do not reliably halt toxin production and shock progresses.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Higher focal organism burden yields higher culture positivity from vagina/wound/NF tissue.
Pigment nephropathy from myoglobinuria contributes substantially to AKI severity.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Streptococcal TSS bacteremic in ~60%, staphylococcal TSS in ~5%.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Pathogen identity strongly drives blood culture yield.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Streptococcal TSS associated with NF in ~50%; rare in menstrual staphylococcal TSS.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Persistent focus sustains pathogen burden despite antibiotics.
Removing tampon, debriding NF, and draining abscess directly resolves source-control failure.
Microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis is a downstream complication of severe DIC.
Multiple-pressor refractory shock is a strong mortality marker.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Constitutive or inducible MLS_B resistance abolishes the toxin-suppression benefit; D-test required.
Without source control, ongoing toxin production overwhelms ribosomal suppression.

side_effects.interpretation: C. difficile colitis risk; usually outweighed by toxin-suppression benefit in TSS.

treatments.context_specific_role: Cornerstone toxin-suppression adjunct in both staphylococcal and streptococcal TSS regardless of β-lactam choice; switches off active toxin synthesis at the 50S ribosome and is unaffected by inoculum size (Eagle effect).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Alternative ribosomal toxin-suppression agent when clindamycin resistance/intolerance is present.

side_effects.interpretation: Reversible myelosuppression, especially with prolonged courses; problematic when DIC coexists.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative ribosomal toxin-suppressor when clindamycin-resistant or unavailable; covers MRSA.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Necessary empiric MRSA coverage until susceptibilities return.

side_effects.interpretation: Nephrotoxicity superimposed on shock-AKI; trough/AUC monitoring required.

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric anti-staphylococcal coverage covering MRSA; should be paired with clindamycin or linezolid for toxin suppression. Cell-wall agents alone do not suppress active toxin elaboration.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: MSSA-targeted β-lactams outperform vancomycin for MSSA bloodstream infection.

side_effects.interpretation: Rare hypersensitivity neutropenia with prolonged β-lactam courses.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive narrow-spectrum coverage for confirmed MSSA TSS; pair with clindamycin/linezolid for toxin suppression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Streptococcal TSS: Group A Streptococcus remains universally penicillin-susceptible.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive antibiotic for streptococcal TSS; combine with clindamycin to overcome the Eagle effect (loss of penicillin efficacy at high inoculum) and to suppress streptococcal exotoxin synthesis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Polymicrobial coverage (gram-negatives, anaerobes) needed in necrotizing fasciitis until pathogen identified.

side_effects.interpretation: Mild AKI synergy with vancomycin reported.

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric broad coverage for suspected necrotizing fasciitis or postoperative TSS until cultures clarify organism; given alongside vancomycin + clindamycin in classic triple regimen.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Strongest evidence in streptococcal TSS; observational benefit on mortality.
Reserved for refractory shock or rapid deterioration despite source control and antibiotics.

side_effects.interpretation: Sucrose-stabilized IVIG products risk osmotic AKI; modern formulations safer.
Volume-load and hyperviscosity may precipitate thrombosis.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive immunomodulation neutralizing circulating superantigens; consider strongly in streptococcal TSS, refractory staphylococcal TSS, and when source control is incomplete or impossible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Massive volume worsens pulmonary capillary leak and pushes toward ARDS; balance with vasopressors after initial resuscitation.

side_effects.interpretation: Pulmonary edema worsens oxygenation, especially in capillary-leak shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line support for distributive shock; TSS often requires 10–20 L in the first 24 h. Balanced crystalloid preferred.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: First-line vasopressor for fluid-refractory distributive shock targeting MAP ≥65 mmHg.

side_effects.interpretation: High-dose pressors plus DIC raise risk of digital/limb ischemia.

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line vasopressor for refractory hypotension; vasopressin and epinephrine are second/third agents.

treatments.drug: Source control intervention (foreign body removal, abscess drainage, surgical debridement)

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antibiotics alone are insufficient for necrotizing fasciitis; emergent operative debridement is the single most life-saving intervention.
Tampon, packing, and retained sponges must be removed immediately to terminate toxin production.

side_effects.interpretation: Operative blood loss; may require transfusion.

treatments.context_specific_role: Single most important intervention together with toxin-suppressing antibiotics; includes tampon/packing removal, abscess drainage, and aggressive serial debridement of necrotizing fasciitis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Indicated for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload, or uremic complications.

side_effects.interpretation: Hemodynamic instability with intermittent HD; CRRT generally better tolerated in shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Continuous RRT preferred in hemodynamically unstable shock-AKI patients with rhabdomyolysis-driven AKI.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ARDSnet protocol (6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤30 cmH₂O) reduces mortality.

treatments.context_specific_role: Lung-protective ventilation for TSS-associated ARDS; prone positioning when PaO₂/FiO₂ <150.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: In refractory septic shock, hydrocortisone shortens shock duration; modest mortality benefit.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct for fluid- and pressor-refractory shock per Surviving Sepsis criteria; not disease-specific to TSS.

current_high_absorbency_tampon_user.trajectory_modulation: Strong driver of menstrual staphylococcal TSS; risk peaks during/just after menses.

postpartum_or_postoperative_within_2_wee.trajectory_modulation: Wound and uterine sources for both staphylococcal and streptococcal TSS.

packing_in_situ.trajectory_modulation: Foreign body acts as toxin-producing focus.

recent_varicella_or_skin_breach.trajectory_modulation: Predisposes to invasive GAS disease and streptococcal TSS, especially in children.

seronegative.trajectory_modulation: ~10% of adults lack anti-TSST-1 antibodies; this group bears nearly all menstrual TSS cases and recurrence risk.

active_IDU.trajectory_modulation: Skin and soft-tissue infection portals for both staphylococcal and streptococcal TSS.

uncontrolled_diabetes.trajectory_modulation: Worse soft tissue infection severity and mortality.

ongoing_NSAID_use.trajectory_modulation: May mask early NF and delay diagnosis; causal role debated.

child_under_10_or_adult_over_65.trajectory_modulation: Higher mortality at age extremes; childhood streptococcal TSS often follows varicella.

supportive_care: Early goal-directed resuscitation: 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid bolus within first 3 hours, often 10–20 L total in first 24 hours given profound capillary leak.
Norepinephrine first-line vasopressor titrated to MAP ≥65 mmHg; add vasopressin and then epinephrine for refractory shock.
ICU admission with continuous hemodynamic monitoring (arterial line, central access, lactate trends).

Empiric triple antimicrobial regimen: vancomycin + clindamycin + piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem; substitute linezolid for clindamycin when MLSB resistance suspected; narrow promptly once organism and susceptibilities are known.
Add penicillin G in confirmed streptococcal TSS, retaining clindamycin for toxin suppression and Eagle-effect mitigation.

Immediate source control: remove tampon, nasal/wound packing, retained foreign bodies; drain abscesses; emergent surgical debridement for any suspected necrotizing fasciitis with serial second-look operations.
Strongly consider IVIG in streptococcal TSS, refractory staphylococcal TSS, or TSS without source control.
Lung-protective mechanical ventilation (6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤30 cmH₂O); prone positioning when PaO₂/FiO₂ <150.

Renal replacement therapy (CRRT preferred in shock) for refractory hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload, or oliguric AKI; aggressive fluid and bicarbonate strategy for rhabdomyolysis-driven AKI.
Aggressive correction of coagulopathy: platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate to replace consumed factors; vigilance for purpura fulminans.
Stress-dose hydrocortisone for fluid- and pressor-refractory shock per Surviving Sepsis criteria.
Glycemic, nutritional, and pressure-injury support; early enteral feeding when feasible.
Discharge counseling on tampon avoidance and recurrence risk, especially in seronegative women; report cluster cases to public health.
Long-term follow-up for delayed sequelae: telogen effluvium, nail dystrophy, neurocognitive impairment, post-ICU syndrome, and limb-functional rehabilitation after necrotizing fasciitis.
